name: Denisovans
hook: A new human lineage identified in 2010 from a finger bone's DNA, before any diagnostic skeleton was found.
claim: In 2010, mtDNA from a Denisova Cave finger bone was reported as a hominin distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans, its divergence initially read as a separate migration out of Africa. Named 'Denisovans' months later from nuclear DNA, before any remains could be diagnosed by anatomy.

claimed_age.label: ~48,000-30,000 years (Denisova 3, by cave stratigraphy)
claimed_age.basis: Age of the finger bone (Denisova 3) as originally reported, inferred from its stratigraphic layer at Denisova Cave, not a direct date on the bone itself.

accepted_age.label: ~52,000-76,000 years (Bayesian model)
accepted_age.basis: Bayesian model combining radiocarbon, U-series, OSL and stratigraphy (Douka et al. 2019); supersedes the 48,000-30,000 yr layer estimate, which Dennell (2019) says was too young for the bone.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Eastern Asian archaic hominins were debated from fragmentary fossils; no archaic Eurasian lineage besides Neanderthals was genetically characterised.

unambiguous_signal.note: A complete mitochondrial genome, then a nuclear genome, matched no known human, Neanderthal or ape sequence; contamination ran up to ~0.4% (mtDNA ~0.1-0.3%, nuclear to 0.43%), too low to explain it.

documented_context.note: The finger bone (Denisova 3) came from an excavated layer at Denisova Cave; its age came from that layer, not a direct date on the bone. Karst deposits can be locally disturbed.

multiple_dating_methods.note: At the time of the claim, the age rested on the radiocarbon-dated stratigraphic sequence alone. Direct multi-method dating of hominin fragments followed only in 2019.

multiple_labs.note: Both 2010 papers sequenced DNA at the same Leipzig (MPI-EVA) facility. Nuclear-genome statistics involved a Harvard co-author (Reich) already part of that consortium paper, not an independent lab.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated by the long-running Russian Academy of Sciences (Siberian Branch) project at Denisova Cave, led by Derevianko, Shunkov and colleagues.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Both founding results appeared as full papers in Nature within the same year (March and December 2010).

material_accessible.note: Sequence data were deposited in public repositories, and specimens curated in Novosibirsk have since been restudied by other groups, e.g. by collagen fingerprinting of further bone fragments.

independent_teams.note: Recovery and sequencing stayed within the Leipzig consortium; but Skoglund & Jakobsson (Uppsala) independently reanalysed the genome within a year, finding further Denisovan affinity in East Asians.

proponent_stake.note: Academic consortium (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology; Harvard Medical School); no commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented in the sources reviewed.

objections.text: The finger bone's original 48,000-30,000 year age came from its stratigraphic layer, not a direct measurement, in a karst cave where deposits can be disturbed by burrowing, subsidence or freeze-thaw.
objections.outcome_note: Douka et al. (2019) modelled the youngest directly-dated Denisovan remains to 52,000-76,000 years, older than the original layer-based estimate; 48,000-30,000 years is no longer used for this bone.

objections.text: Krause et al.'s reading of the mtDNA split as evidence for a distinct hominin migration out of Africa was an over-interpretation; the divergence need not imply a separate migration.
objections.outcome_note: Reich et al.'s nuclear genome, published later the same year, placed Denisovans as sister to Neanderthals rather than a separate deep migration, dropping the reading this objection challenged.

objections.text: Denisovans were named from molecular data alone with no morphological holotype of their own; only a handful of fragmentary remains from one site were attributed to them for their first decade.
objections.outcome_note: Xiahe, Penghu and Harbin fossils now corroborate the lineage by protein or DNA evidence. Homo longi (2021) and Homo juluensis (2024) have been proposed as binomials, but neither is in consensus use.

objections.text: Denisovan and Neanderthal genetic affinities with living humans could reflect shared ancestral variation retained from a common ancestor, not introgression from real interbreeding.
objections.raised_by: Lowery, Uribe, Jimenez, Weiss et al. (2013)
objections.outcome_note: A directly sequenced first-generation Neanderthal-Denisovan hybrid (Denisova 11, 2018) shows these lineages did interbreed; no later paper defending the shared-ancestral-polymorphism reading was found.

objections.text: The Xiahe mandible was a surface find handed to researchers by a monk in 1980 with no excavation record; its ~160,000-year age comes from U-series dating of a carbonate crust on the bone, not the bone itself.
objections.outcome_note: The protein-based Denisovan identification of the mandible is not disputed, but its own age remains an inference from the adhering crust rather than a direct measurement; no subsequent direct date was found.

status_note: A genetically distinct Denisovan lineage is accepted across paleoanthropology, attested at Denisova Cave, Baishiya, Penghu and Harbin. The 2010 result was accepted quickly, not independently replicated; rank and naming remain debated.
what_settled_it: Mitochondrial and nuclear genome analyses of the same bone, both from the Leipzig-based consortium, agreed months apart in 2010 that it matched no known population and, via the nuclear genome, showed ancestry in living Melanesians. Later finds corroborated but did not independently replicate it.

timeline.event: A monk finds a hominin mandible at Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe, on the Tibetan Plateau, China, later called the Xiahe mandible.
A hominin finger-bone fragment, later named Denisova 3, is excavated at Denisova Cave.
Krause et al. sequence its complete mitochondrial genome and report a lineage unlike Neanderthals or modern humans.
Reich et al. sequence the nuclear genome, name the group 'Denisovans', and detect ~4-6% Denisovan ancestry in present-day Melanesians.
Slon et al. recover Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA directly from cave sediment with no skeletal remains, a method later applied at Baishiya.
Slon et al. sequence 'Denisova 11', a first-generation daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
Chen et al. identify the Xiahe mandible as Denisovan by ancient protein analysis, the first Denisovan fossil outside Denisova Cave.
Douka, Jacobs et al. use Bayesian-modelled radiocarbon and optical dating to show hominin occupation at Denisova Cave extends back at least 200,000 years.
Zhang et al. detect Denisovan mtDNA in Baishiya sediment, corroborating Denisovan presence there; authors overlap with the Denisova Cave team.
Ji, Wu et al. describe the Harbin cranium as a new species, 'Homo longi', with no molecular link to Denisovans.
Fu et al. identify the Harbin cranium as Denisovan via mtDNA from dental calculus and, in a companion paper, ancient proteins; both led by the same team.
Tsutaya et al. identify the Penghu 1 mandible from Taiwan as a male Denisovan by ancient protein analysis, a fourth Denisovan locality.

decisive_tests.test: Recover nuclear DNA or a proteome from additional Xiahe-, Penghu- or Harbin-associated skeletal material to build a second high-coverage Denisovan genome outside Denisova Cave.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the Tibetan, Taiwanese and Northeast Asian Denisovan populations were genetically distinct from the Siberian lineage, and would support formally naming the group.

falsifier: Independent reanalysis showing the Denisova 3 sequences were contaminated or artefactual, or repeated failure to replicate Denisovan DNA or proteins in the Siberian, Tibetan, Taiwanese or Harbin material, would overturn this status. No such failure is reported.

sources.citation: Krause, J., Fu, Q., Good, J.M., Viola, B. et al. (2010). The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia. Nature 464(7290): 894-897.
sources.note: Abstract read in full: mtDNA from the Denisova finger bone, excavated 2008, dated 48,000-30,000 yr by stratigraphy; lineage distinct from Neanderthal/modern human out-of-Africa migrations.

sources.citation: Reich, D., Green, R.E., Kircher, M., Krause, J. et al. (2010). Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia. Nature 468(7327): 1053-1060.
sources.note: Full introduction/results sections read: names 'Denisovans', reports ~4-6% Melanesian ancestry, discusses mtDNA-vs-nuclear divergence discrepancy, and gives contamination estimates (~0.1-0.4%).

sources.citation: Chen, F., Welker, F., Shen, C., Bailey, S.E. et al. (2019). A late Middle Pleistocene Denisovan mandible from the Tibetan Plateau. Nature 569(7756): 409-412.
sources.note: Read in full: mandible identified by ancient protein analysis at Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe; acknowledgements confirm it was provided by an anonymous monk; U-series dating used a carbonate crust.

sources.citation: Zhang, D., Xia, H., Chen, F., Li, B. et al. (2020). Denisovan DNA in Late Pleistocene sediments from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau. Science 370(6516): 584-587.
sources.note: Abstract read: Denisovan mitochondrial DNA recovered from Baishiya sediment, indicating presence at about 100, 60 and possibly 45 thousand years ago.

sources.citation: Fu, Q., Cao, P., Dai, Q., Bennett, E.A. et al. (2025). Denisovan mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus of the >146,000-year-old Harbin cranium. Cell 188(15): 3919-3926.e9.
sources.note: Abstract read: no DNA from tooth or petrous bone, but mtDNA from dental calculus falls within Denisovan variation, related to an early Siberian Denisovan branch.

sources.citation: Ji, Q., Wu, W., Ji, Y., Li, Q. et al. (2021). Late Middle Pleistocene Harbin cranium represents a new Homo species. The Innovation 2(3): 100132.
sources.note: Abstract read: proposes the Harbin cranium as a new Homo species (Homo longi) based on morphology; no DNA/protein evidence and no Denisovan link in this paper.

sources.citation: Peyrégne, S., Slon, V., Kelso, J. (2024). More than a decade of genetic research on the Denisovans. Nature Reviews Genetics 25(2): 83-103.
sources.note: Abstract open, full text paywalled. Confirms only ~10 fragmentary remains from two sites attributed to Denisovans by molecular data alone as of this review.

sources.citation: Slon, V., Mafessoni, F., Vernot, B., de Filippo, C. et al. (2018). The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Nature 561(7721): 113-116.
sources.note: Full text (PMC) read: Denisova 11 is a first-generation Neanderthal-Denisovan offspring, ~38.6% Neanderthal-like and ~42.3% Denisovan-like informative alleles.

sources.citation: Douka, K., Slon, V., Jacobs, Z., Ramsey, C.B. et al. (2019). Age estimates for hominin fossils and the onset of the Upper Palaeolithic at Denisova Cave. Nature 565(7741): 640-644.
sources.note: Abstract/intro accessible; full text and dating figures paywalled. The 52,000-76,000 yr range in accepted_age follows the skeptic review's verified reading, not re-confirmed this pass.

sources.citation: Jacobs, Z., Li, B., Shunkov, M.V., Kozlikin, M.B. et al. (2019). Timing of archaic hominin occupation of Denisova Cave in southern Siberia. Nature 565(7741): 594-599.
sources.note: Abstract accessible, full text paywalled: prior chronology relied on radiocarbon (to ~50 ka) plus less reliable TL/palaeomagnetism/genetics; this paper adds 103 OSL dates.

sources.citation: Dennell, R. (2019). Dating of hominin discoveries at Denisova. Nature 565(7741): 571-572.
sources.note: Read in full (News & Views): cave occupied >=200,000 yr; excavations began ~1979; notes karst deposits can be disturbed by burrowing, subsidence and freeze-thaw.

sources.citation: Fu, Q., Bai, F., Rao, H., Chen, S. et al. (2025). The proteome of the late Middle Pleistocene Harbin individual. Science 389(6761): 704-707.
sources.note: Abstract read in full: 95 endogenous proteins from the Harbin cranium; 3 Denisovan-derived amino-acid variants; clusters with Denisova 3. Confirms protein AND mtDNA (S5) identification.

sources.citation: Martinón-Torres, M., Dennell, R., Bermúdez de Castro, J.M. (2011). The Denisova hominin need not be an out of Africa story. Journal of Human Evolution 60(2): 251-255.
sources.note: Crossref metadata confirmed; no open abstract found. Title disputes Krause et al.'s out-of-Africa migration reading of the mtDNA result.

sources.citation: Lowery, R.K., Uribe, G., Jimenez, E.B., Weiss, M.A. et al. (2013). Neanderthal and Denisova genetic affinities with contemporary humans: Introgression versus common ancestral polymorphisms. Gene 530(1): 83-94.
sources.note: Crossref metadata confirmed; no open abstract found. Title matches: archaic-human affinities could reflect shared ancestral polymorphism, not introgression.

sources.citation: Tsutaya, T., Sawafuji, R., Taurozzi, A.J., Fagernäs, Z. et al. (2025). A male Denisovan mandible from Pleistocene Taiwan. Science 388(6743): 176-180.
sources.note: Abstract read in full: Penghu 1 mandible ID'd as male Denisovan via 2 Denisovan-specific amino-acid variants from 4,241 residues; age 10-70 or 130-190 ka.

sources.citation: Skoglund, P., Jakobsson, M. (2011). Archaic human ancestry in East Asia. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 108(45): 18301-18306.
sources.note: Abstract read in full: independent Uppsala analysis, within a year of Reich et al. 2010, found Denisovan affinity in East/Southeast Asians beyond Oceania.

sources.citation: Bae, C.J., Wu, X. (2024). Making sense of eastern Asian Late Quaternary hominin variability. Nature Communications 15(1).
sources.note: Abstract read: reviews named eastern Asian hominin groups, including Homo longi and Homo juluensis alongside H. floresiensis and H. luzonensis.

confidence_note: Founding, hybrid, Xiahe, Baishiya, Penghu and Harbin-proteome papers read as full text or full abstracts. S7/S9/S10 are paywalled beyond abstracts ('exists'); two 2011-13 critiques are metadata-only.
corrections: The widely cited 48,000-30,000 year age for Denisova 3 was a stratigraphic estimate, not a direct measurement; Douka et al. (2019) modelled the youngest Denisovan remains to 52,000-76,000 years, older than its layer implied.
notes: This record treats 2010-2025 as one case: later specimens (Xiahe, Penghu, Harbin) corroborate the 2010 claim but share investigators with the Leipzig consortium, so they are corroboration, not independent replication. Puzzle: 2010 mtDNA implied a split twice as deep as the Neanderthal-human split; the nuclear genome, months later, placed Denisovans as Neanderthals sister, so mtDNA reflected lineage history, not divergence time. No binomial is in consensus use: Homo longi (2021) and Homo juluensis (2024) have been proposed for populations that may include Denisovans. No sustained rebuttal of the lineage existence was found: fast acceptance of a surprise discovery, not a contested anomaly.

open_issues: Declined to add Meyer et al. 2012 (Science, high-coverage genome) as a separate source; budget did not allow verifying it, and S2/S8 already establish the founding genome and hybrid evidence.

Martinón-Torres et al. (2011) and Lowery et al. (2013) could not be read beyond Crossref metadata (paywalled, no open abstract); marked 'exists', with outcomes reasoned from related checked sources (S2, S8), not each paper's own text.

The 52,000-76,000 year range in accepted_age (S9) follows the task brief and the skeptic's verified Europe PMC reading; this pass's own fetch of the publisher page truncated before that figure, so S9 stays 'exists' rather than 're-checked'.
Declined to add Wikimedia Commons plates; still no confirmed file titles found, and none attempted this pass under the tool-call budget.

Declined to add a separate objection on Harbin's and Penghu's own lack of excavation context (both are non-stratified finds like Xiahe); noted here for a future revision rather than added under length budgets.
